backend._reload_note: BUG FOUND 2026-09-03 (user report: fixed testing devteam login doesn't work on the installer). This base file is what the PACKAGED DESKTOP APP actually reads -- electron/main.js deliberately sets APP_ENV=desktop, which matches neither config.development.json nor config.production.json, so it falls through to plain config.json (same reason APP_ENV=desktop exists at all; see that file's own comment). reload=true belongs ONLY in config.development.json (which already has its own correct copy of this key and overrides this one for local dev, where APP_ENV defaults to 'development'). It makes uvicorn run a supervisor + a SEPARATE multiprocessing worker process; Electron's killAll() only tracks the supervisor it spawned, not that worker, so any relaunch, crash-recovery, or reinstall on a machine that ran an earlier build could leave an orphaned worker still bound to port 8000 -- silently serving stale data (a different DB connection, a devteam account from whatever session created it) while the dashboard happily talks to it, mistaking it for the current app. Reproduced firsthand: identical orphaned-worker chatter happened repeatedly while testing this exact fix.

database._type_note: This key is DOCUMENTATION ONLY -- nothing reads it. It said 'postgres' while every standalone run used SQLite, which is the kind of mismatch that costs an hour when someone trusts it. The real switch is the DATABASE_URL environment variable, read in app/db.py: set -> Postgres, unset -> SQLite. A packaged install must leave it UNSET.
database._path_note: BUG FOUND 2026-08-19: 'path' below is ALSO dead -- db.py's SQLite branch never reads database.path at all, it opens ECOVISION_WRITABLE_DIR/ecovision.db directly (flat, no subfolder). backend.py used to compute its own DATA_DIR from this key too, but that DATA_DIR/DB_PATH pair was itself unused dead code (removed) -- its only real effect was silently creating an empty, never-written writable-dir/data/ folder on every startup, which is why this specific field looked load-bearing but wasn't. Left here as a record, not a live setting.
database._offline: Fully local by design: SQLite file on disk, no network calls, no cloud service. If Supabase is adopted later it would replace the db.py backend behind the same interface; offline-first would need its local cache, since this system must keep detecting when the link drops.

detection._models_note: The old detection.models block was removed: nothing read it. The pose weights are resolved by load_model_with_fallback() in maincode/main.py, which prefers yolo11s-pose.engine and falls back to the .pt; the violence weights come from detection.violence.model_path and detection.violence.scene_model_path below. violence._scene_person_confirm: Added 2026-10-01. Each check also scores crops around the groups of people the pose model found (aspect-matched, so they look like whole frames to the model), and the value that goes through smoothing/confirmation is min(whole-frame confidence, best crop over the last 3 checks): the scene AND some group of real people must both look violent. That removes enough false alarms to drop consecutive 3 -> 2, which is what buys back recall. MEASURED on identical footage, same daynight weights, all six rows from one trace (experiments/crop_recheck in the training repo): spliced_recall_200 (200 held-out fights from 200 different source videos spliced into street footage) + 2 h of the four held-out real cameras (30 min each). whole frame 0.50/3 (previous deployment): 75.0% caught, 5.0 false alarms/hr. whole frame 0.50/2: 83.0%, 12.0/hr. CONFIRMED 0.50/2 (this setting): 79.0%, 3.0/hr -- better on both axes. confirmed 0.50/1: 81.0%, 5.0/hr. confirmed 0.40/2: 82.0%, 8.0/hr. Per camera at this setting: flyover 12 -> 12/hr, market 0, iloilo 0, lyns_restaurant 8 -> 0/hr. Also measured: using the crop to ADD detections ('or') gave the same recall at 3-6x the false alarms, so the crop only ever vetoes. On 75 real CCTV fights / 73 non-fights from SurvFight sources that share nothing with training, single-reading clip FPR falls 31.5% -> 21.9% for recall 81.3% -> 77.3%. The shipped SceneViolenceDetector was checked against the experiment check by check (verify_shipped.py): identical values on 720 checks. COST: one batched X3D forward of 1 + up to 5 clips per check instead of 1. ROLLBACK: set scene_person_confirm to false AND scene_consecutive_required back to 3 -- the two are a pair; confirmation off at 2 is the 12 alarms/hr row above.
violence._scene_consecutive_required_rollback: Was 1. Raised to 3 on 2026-08-14. TWO separate things are fixed by this. (1) A MEASUREMENT/CONFIG MISMATCH: eval_false_alarms_corpus.py defaults to --consecutive 2, but main.py:495 builds SceneViolenceDetector() with no consecutive argument, so the live system used this config value of 1. Every false-alarm figure on record -- including the 32.0 alarms/hr for corpus_neg and 41.0 for ucf_neg_motion -- was therefore measured at 2 while deployment ran at 1. Replayed at 1, the deployed model gives 49.0 alarms/hr (flyover 38, market 2, lyns 9), so the published rates understated live behaviour by ~53%. (2) THE SETTING ITSELF: consecutive_required has never been tunable, because 5-second benchmark clips yield too few inference points for need>=3 to succeed arithmetically -- a property of the clips, not the model. Measured instead on continuous footage (build_spliced_recall_set.py: 40 held-out violent test clips spliced into real Davao night street footage with 25 s of ordinary activity either side, replayed through the shipped _smooth_and_confirm): at threshold 0.50, cons=1 and cons=2 and cons=3 all detect 38/40 events (95.0%), while held-out camera alarms fall 49.0 -> 32.0 -> 17.0 per hour. cons=4 drops to 36/40 (90.0%) for 9.0/hr. So 3 is the last free step and 4 is the first one that costs. CAVEATS: 40 events gives about +/-2.5 points of resolution, so 'zero cost' means 'lost none of 40', not 'provably lossless'; and spliced recall is an UPPER bound, because a hard cut between two cameras is itself a large visual change and the violent clips are benchmark footage (several are indoor, some carry YouTube compilation watermarks and one a visible player UI). To roll back, set this to 1 for the previous deployed behaviour, or 2 to match how every historical measurement was taken.
violence._scene_no_person_fallback: Added 2026-10-07. With person-crop confirmation an alarm needs a crop around people; when the pose model finds NOBODY for 6 checks (~3 s) -- blurry, dark or distant footage -- there is nothing to confirm with, and 7 of the 24 fights the deployed setting missed were vetoed exactly that way. Then a whole-frame score >= 0.8 counts on its own. Setting chosen on 2 h of held-out cameras (88.0 -> 90.0% caught, no extra alarms) and CONFIRMED on 5 h, 3 h of which did not exist when it was chosen: 88.0% -> 90.0% of 200 fights, 1.40 -> 1.40 false alarms/hr (7 alarms either way). Every setting with min_scene >= 0.8 gained 1-2 points with no extra alarm; 0.7 added one. Rollback: set min_scene to null.
violence._scene_ensemble_paths: Added 2026-10-05. A second whole-frame checkpoint (the ucabal recipe retrained with 6 false-alarm clips mined from TRAINING cameras added as negatives) runs on the same clip and the two models' calibrated probabilities are averaged (SceneViolenceDetector._forward). Alone it is not better than ucabal (83.5% vs 86.5% at 0.50/2); averaged, the two disagree on different false alarms. MEASURED through the app's own code path (trace_crop.py --ensemble; identical to the offline average) on spliced_recall_200 + 2 h of the four held-out cameras, person-crop confirmed: ucabal alone 0.50/2: 86.5% caught, 2.0 false alarms/hr; ensemble 0.45/2: 88.0%, 2.0/hr; ensemble 0.50/2: 85.5%, 0.5/hr. 1,310 test clips at 0.45: accuracy 93.1%, recall 92.8%, precision 93.4% (ucabal at 0.50: 92.8 / 92.2 / 93.4). Cost: a second X3D-XS forward per check. Rollback: scene_ensemble_paths [] and scene_confidence_threshold 0.5.
violence._scene_model_path_ucabal: Deployed 2026-10-03, replacing daynight. Same recipe as daynight (fine-tuned from corpus_neg, 2 blocks unfrozen), data = daynight's manifest PLUS UCF-Crime clips cut at the event timestamps of the UCA annotations (CVPR 2024): 821 fight clips from 98 Fighting/Assault/Abuse videos and 835 calm clips from the non-violent stretches of the same and of robbery/vandalism videos -- same shops, restaurants and streets on both sides. Best epoch 7 of 10. MEASURED at the live rule (person-crop confirmed, 0.50, 2 in a row): spliced_recall_200 79.0% -> 86.5%; held-out real cameras 3.0 -> 2.0 false alarms/hr (flyover 12 -> 6, iloilo 0 -> 2, restaurant 0 -> 0, market 0 -> 0). Unseen SurvFight real-CCTV clips (peak reading): recall 77.3% -> 78.7%, FPR 21.9% -> 24.7% (2 clips of 73, noise). CAVEAT: on 507 held-out UCF clips (live rule) fights alarmed 23.8% -> 31.6% but calm indoor clips alarmed 4.0% -> 8.0% -- indoor shop/restaurant CCTV may see more alerts; street cameras did not. The unbalanced version (279 calm clips) was measured and rejected: 89.5% caught at 13.0 false alarms/hr. ROLLBACK: weights/x3d_xs_violence_scene_daynight.pt (nothing else changes).

Recall UNCHANGED at 95.0% (38/40 on the spliced replay, deployed operating point 0.50/consecutive=3) while real-camera alarms fall 12.75 -> 4.50/hr (flyover 45 -> 6/hr is nearly the whole effect; lyns_restaurant is the one camera that gets WORSE, 6 -> 12/hr -- not a uniform win, see the checkpoint's own .meta.json for the full breakdown including the 0.45 threshold that was measured and rejected). weapon._model_path_v3: weapons v3 deployed 2026-10-03, replacing v2, and runs at imgsz 960 (maincode/detection_rules.py WEAPON_IMGSZ). Fine-tuned from v2 at 960 on v2's training images PLUS 7,500 synthetic street-camera frames (build_synth_weapons.py in the training repo): 5,000 frames of our own Davao street footage with real gun/knife cut-outs pasted at the wrists of real people at street-camera size, and 2,500 untouched frames from the same cameras. None of the 8 false-alarm test cameras or 4 held-out cameras were used as backgrounds; val/test are v2's, 100% real. Best epoch 16 of a run stopped at 17 (out-of-memory crash, not a plateau). MEASURED, both models at 960 and the deployed gun 0.30 / knife 0.23 gates: (1) false weapons on 4 h of daytime street footage with no weapons in it, after the live static-object filter and tracking: v2 909/hr -> v3 112/hr (false gun detections 6,764 -> 372). (2) recall by weapon size on the 2,157-image test split: guns 5-10% of frame 39.8% -> 39.4%, 10-20% 73.1% -> 65.9%, 40%+ 90.1% -> 89.6%; knives 5-10% 75.7% -> 83.8%. So: the same guns found (slightly fewer mid-size ones), 8x fewer false weapons. Versus v2 as it actually ran (640), small-gun recall 14% -> 39%. ROLLBACK: model_path weights/weapons_v2.pt AND WEAPON_IMGSZ 640 -- a pair.
weapon._why_no_smoothing: Single-frame YOLO object detector, not the temporal SceneViolenceDetector the other three classes use -- there is no multi-frame confirmation to tune. consecutive_required=1 documents that plainly rather than implying a EMA/smoothing stage that doesn't exist for this class.
weapon._added: 2026-08-19: previously ran unconditionally with no enable/disable switch anywhere in the app -- added for parity with violence/robbery/vandalism, all of which already had one. See maincode/main.py's WEAPON_DETECTION_ENABLED gate on the _weapon_exec submit call.
weapon._per_class_thresholds: The 0.38 above is a legacy top-level fallback, not what's actually enforced -- CONF_BY_CLASS in maincode/detection_rules.py applies gun 0.30, knife 0.23 per detection (since weapons v2, 21 Aug; was Gun 0.52, Knife 0.45, Sign 0.40), and WEAPON_YOLO_CONF_FLOOR takes the min of those and this value so YOLO's own conf= cutoff never discards a detection a per-class check would have kept. A bug found 19 Aug had this backwards (YOLO's conf= used the flat 0.6 top-level value directly, silently dropping every Knife/Sign detection between 0.40 and 0.60 before the per-class check ever saw them -- 11 of 58 in a 60-image sample); fixed by routing through the min().

weapon._model_path_rollback: weapons v2 deployed 2026-08-21, replacing weapon_signs.pt. THE PREVIOUS MODEL'S PUBLISHED METRICS WERE WITHDRAWN, not adjusted: its train/val/test splits shared 99.4% / 14.6% / 12.0% of base images (Roboflow ships ~2.8 augmented copies per source photo and the split was made at FILE level), so validation was very nearly a copy of training and every early-stopping decision against it was noise. Its 88.7% headline recall was further inflated by a traffic-sign class scoring ~100%. v2 is split by BASE IMAGE with 0/0/0 overlap, verified independently by verify_all_leakage.py. Classes gun/knife/phone; the sign class is gone. MEASURED on the 2,157-image leakage-free test split at imgsz 640, epoch 98 of 120: 79.7% recall / 85.0% accuracy / 99.6% precision / 0.9% FPR at the OLD thresholds, and 89.0% recall @ 3.1% FPR at the new gun 0.30 / knife 0.23 (chosen on val, reported on test). To roll back, set this to weights/weapon_signs.pt AND restore main.py's WEAPON_IMGSZ to 416 and CONF_BY_CLASS to gun 0.52 / knife 0.45 -- the three changes are a set and rolling back only one produces a configuration that was never measured. Backup: weights/_backup_20260821/.

robbery._confidence_threshold_085: Raised 0.70 -> 0.85 on 2026-10-03. MEASURED on 2 h of the four held-out real cameras (nothing criminal in them), consecutive 3: 0.70 -> 12.0 false alarms/hr (market camera 28/hr, restaurant 12, iloilo 6, flyover 2); 0.85 -> 0.5/hr (one alarm in 2 h). Clip recall on the 183-clip test split (8 source scenes) in the same harness: 54.2% -> 39.8%; clip FPR 7.0% -> 3.0%. A detector that fires 12 times an hour on empty streets trains operators to ignore it, so fewer, rarer, more trustworthy alerts is the better trade until real robbery footage from our own cameras exists. A retrain on 737 UCF robbery clips (+ fights as negatives) was measured the same day and rejected: 13.3% recall, 17.5 false alarms/hr. ROLLBACK: 0.70.
robbery._why_0_7: HISTORY -- threshold raised to 0.85 on 2026-10-03 (see _confidence_threshold_085). Chosen from the held-out test sweep, not by default. On 139 clips from EIGHT source videos the model never trained on: at 0.5 it scores 76.3% accuracy / 79.6% recall / 62.9% precision / 25.6% FPR; at 0.7, 84.2% / 65.3% / 86.5% / 5.6%; at 0.8, 84.2% / 57.1% / 96.6% / 1.1%. 0.7 is where precision becomes usable without collapsing recall. A quarter of normal clips misfiring at 0.5 would make the class ignorable, which is the failure mode this project spent the most effort on for violence.
robbery._consecutive_3: Matches the violence detector. Measured there on continuous spliced footage: cons 1->3 removed 65% of false alarms while losing none of 40 events. Not separately measured for robbery -- there is no continuous robbery footage to measure it on -- so it is carried over as the safer default rather than claimed as tuned.
robbery._replaces: RULE_ROBBERY_PLACEHOLDER_CONF = 0.895 in maincode/main.py, an invented constant sent to the dashboard whenever the ARMED-person-near-another-person heuristic fired. There was no derivation for 0.895. The model emits a real probability.
robbery._caveat: Trained on 26 source videos, tested on 8. Any figure here is a measurement over 8 scenes, not 139 independent samples. Largely UCF-Crime footage: driveways, car parks and shop interiors, not Philippine streets. Recall on the deployment cameras is unmeasured, as it is for violence.
robbery._rollback: Set enabled=false to return to the rule-based path.

vandalism._why_disabled: HISTORY (Aug 2026) -- vandalism has been ENABLED since 22 Aug and person-crop confirmed since 4 Oct (see _person_confirm, _why_enabled). MEASURED, TWICE, ON TWO DIFFERENT ROUTES -- this class is disabled on evidence, not assumption. (1) TRAINED MODEL, retrained 2026-08-21 on 26 source videos (was 11). The retrain WORKED in the sense that mattered: 82.4% accuracy against a 62.7% majority baseline on a 5-scene held-out test split, where the previous model scored 70.3% against a 78.4% baseline, i.e. 8.1 points BELOW guessing. The class now carries positive information. It is still disabled because the number that decides deployability is not per-clip accuracy but false alarms per HOUR on real cameras: replayed through the shipped smoothing at the deployed threshold 0.5 / consecutive 3 over 20 minutes of each of four held-out cameras, it produced 167 alarms in 1.33 hours = 125.25/hr (agdao_flyover 195, lyns_restaurant 177, agdao_market 78, iloilo_guiez 51). The deployed violence detector runs at 4.50/hr. This is 28x worse -- a false alert every 29 seconds. No operator would keep reading them. (2) RULE-BASED ROUTE, instrumented per condition on 48 graffiti clips: 0.0% recall with the original 'sign' gate (that class fired 0 times in 3,600 frames -- structurally impassable, not mistuned), rising to only 8.3% once a purpose-trained graffiti detector replaced it. Per-condition counts show why: 3,231 person-frames fail the wrist-near-mark test even after a mark is detected somewhere in frame. The rule keys on the RESIDUE of the act, and while someone is spraying the mark does not exist yet. (3) A change-detection prototype (detect the mark APPEARING in a cell that was empty during a baseline) reached 3 of 4 events but false-alarmed on all four held-out cameras. Also disabled.
vandalism._why_no_model_either: HISTORY (Aug 2026) -- vandalism has been ENABLED since 22 Aug and person-crop confirmed since 4 Oct (see _person_confirm, _why_enabled). A trained X3D vandalism model was also built and rejected: 87.5% FPR on the held-out scenes, firing on 7 of 8 normal clips, with 70.3% accuracy against a 78.4% base rate -- worse than labelling everything vandalism. Trained on 11 scenes. Robbery works at 26. Scene count is the blocker.
vandalism._to_enable: HISTORY (Aug 2026; enabled since) -- still the lever for better recall: More SCENES -- not more epochs, and not a different architecture. Train accuracy reached 89.3% while validation sat near 60%, so capacity is already being spent memorising the 16 training scenes. Public data is exhausted: NWPU Campus (28 classes), UBnormal (22) and XD-Violence (6) contain no vandalism class at all, and MSAD -- the only dataset that does -- covers glass and doors, i.e. property destruction rather than marking. There is NO public video dataset of the graffiti act. See docs/related_work_notes.md Part II section 5. The remaining lever is docs/vandalism_data_collection.md: ~20 filmed outdoor locations.
vandalism._dashboard_note: HISTORY (Aug 2026) -- vandalism has been ENABLED since 22 Aug and person-crop confirmed since 4 Oct (see _person_confirm, _why_enabled). With this false, no VANDALISM alert is emitted at all. That is deliberate: the alternative was RULE_VANDALISM_PLACEHOLDER_CONF = 0.84, an invented constant rendered on the dashboard identically to a real model output, attached to a rule that cannot fire.

vandalism._marks_model_path_rollback: graffiti v2 deployed 2026-08-21, replacing vandalism_marks.pt. Both models were scored in ONE run on the SAME untouched 165-image leakage-free test split, so the comparison cannot drift across sessions: v2 mAP50 0.734 / mAP50-95 0.485 / P 0.804 / R 0.646 versus v1 0.718 / 0.472 / 0.794 / 0.602 -- better on all four, no metric traded against another. Trained on 7,943 images (was 1,177) by combining the 17K-Graffiti Universe mirror with the civic-issues corpus; 0% base-image overlap between corpora and 0 bases straddling any split (verify_all_leakage.py). Trained at imgsz 416 deliberately, matching VANDAL_MARK_IMGSZ in main.py. HONEST SCALE OF THE WIN: 6.75x more data bought +1.6 points of mAP50 -- the new corpus is photographer-framed (median box 18.5% of frame vs 4.9% in the CCTV-like data), so the bottleneck is scale-matched data, not quantity. To roll back, set this to weights/vandalism_marks.pt (kept on disk, also in weights/_backup_20260821/).
vandalism._v3_result: vandalism v3 trained 2026-08-22: added 700 train / 150 val REAL DAVAO STREET clips as negatives (v2 had none -- all 145 of its negatives were non-crime spans of the same UCF videos). Split BY CAMERA, with the two corpus cameras that are also held-out evaluation cameras excluded. RESULT: false alarms fall 125.25 -> 21.75/hr, a 5.8x reduction (flyover 195->72, market 78->9, iloilo 51->0, lyns 177->6). agdao_market and lyns_restaurant were NEVER in training, so their 8.7x and 29.5x improvements are generalisation to unseen cameras. COST: UCF test recall 93.8% -> 87.5% and test FPR 36.8% -> 52.6%; that split contains no Davao footage so it cannot measure what the negatives fixed, but the regression is real and stated. TWO GUARDS were required to make this trustworthy: with 148 positives against 796 negatives, unweighted loss and raw-accuracy checkpoint selection would have saved the most COLLAPSED model as best (predicting 'never' scores 82.2% on that val split). Trained with --class-weights auto and --select-metric balanced; per-class recall at the chosen epoch was neg 86.7% / pos 84.6%, confirming no collapse. STILL DISABLED: 21.75/hr against the violence detector's 4.50/hr.
vandalism._threshold_note: HISTORY (Aug 2026) -- threshold is now 0.60 with person-crop confirmation (see _person_confirm). 0.7, chosen by measuring false alarms per HOUR on four real held-out cameras rather than by per-clip accuracy. At 0.5 v3 produces 21.75/hr; at 0.7 it produces 6.75/hr (flyover 24.0, market 3.0, iloilo 0.0, lyns 0.0) for 78.1% recall on the held-out test split. The deployed violence detector runs at 4.50/hr, so this is the first vandalism configuration that is in the same league as something already accepted in production. Raising to 0.8 would cut recall to 62.5% and is not worth it; dropping to 0.5 triples the alarm rate.
vandalism._why_enabled: ENABLED 2026-08-22, after being disabled since the class was first built. The whole journey, because the reason matters more than the number: (1) the rule-based route scored 0% recall -- its gate depended on a detector class that fired 0 times in 3,600 frames, so no threshold could have rescued it; (2) replacing that gate with a purpose-trained graffiti detector lifted it only to 8.3%, because the rule keys on the RESIDUE of the act and the mark does not exist while it is being made; (3) a detector-only signal reached 20.8%, still at the majority baseline; (4) change detection caught 3 of 4 events but alarmed on every camera; (5) the trained model at 11 scenes scored BELOW its own always-guess baseline. What finally worked was none of those: raising the scene count 11 -> 26 made the class carry positive information, and adding real Davao street footage as negatives cut false alarms 125.25 -> 21.75 -> 6.75/hr at threshold 0.7. Kept experimental=true because the test split is FIVE scenes; set enabled=false to revert.

verifier._backend: gpu = transformers fp16 on the GPU (~4.2 GB VRAM, ~7 s per check, detectors drop to ~2 FPS during a check). cpu = llama.cpp's llama-server with a 4-bit GGUF, started and stopped by the AI core (~2.1 GB RAM, no VRAM, ~15 s per check, detectors keep ~85% of their frame rate). auto = gpu if min_free_vram_gb is free at load time, else cpu. Default auto since 2026-10-08: where the gpu fits it is identical to gpu; where it does not (a 4 GB card, a game open) gpu leaves the verifier off -- the strict settings, fights 88.0% at 1.4/hr -- while auto verifies on the cpu (fights 91.0% at 0.2/hr with re-checks). Measured on 5 h of held-out cameras, fights at 0.25 x1, cut-off cross-validated by source video: gpu 90.5% caught at 0.4 false alarms/hr (AUC 0.996), cpu 89.0% at 0.2/hr (AUC 0.992). The shipped app server code reproduces the experiment's scores exactly (experiments/crop_recheck/verify_cpu_backend_shipped.py: 12/12 alarms, max difference 0.000).

cpu._threads: null = half the logical cores (6 of 12 here, which is what was measured). llama.cpp CPU build b11459; it runs at below-normal priority with its prompt cache off (the default 8 GB cache grew it from 2 to 10 GB of committed memory and was never reused).

verifier._reason: Off since 2026-10-07: writing the one-sentence description roughly doubled each check (6.5 s -> 14-15 s on the GTX 1660 SUPER), and while a check runs the detector drops from ~15 to ~2 FPS. The yes/no verdict alone is what the measurements are based on.
verifier._ram_guard: Before loading, system memory is checked per backend (alarm_verifier.AlarmVerifier.MEMORY_NEEDS_GB; override with ram_guard.<gpu|cpu>.{physical_gb, commit_gb}). Measured 2026-10-07 on top of a running AI core: gpu backend +1.3 GB physical RAM at peak but +5.3 GB COMMITTED (RAM + page file; +4.0 GB kept), cpu backend ~2.1 GB of both. Needs with margin: gpu 1.8 GB physical / 5.8 GB commit headroom, cpu 2.6 / 2.6. The commit limit is what an oversized load breaks (it crashed the detection loop once). Replaced a single 3.0 GB physical-RAM check, which was too strict for the gpu backend and blind to commit.
verifier._vram_guard: The verifier loads load_delay_seconds after start-up, once the detectors have loaded and run, and only if at least min_free_vram_gb of GPU memory is free then (measured peak ~4.16 GB for Qwen3-VL-2B fp16). Otherwise backend gpu stays off (the detectors keep their strict settings, exactly the system before verification existed) and backend auto uses the cpu backend, which has its own RAM guard (_ram_guard).

violence._recheck_seconds: Added 2026-10-07. While a candidate stays on, unverified and with no check pending, it is checked again every 7 s (alarm_verifier.VerifiedGate). 8 of the 15 fights that got no check at 0.25 x1 began while a candidate was already on, so they had no rising edge of their own. Cross-validated on 200 fights + 5 h of held-out cameras: one check per candidate 90.5% at 0.4/hr; re-check every 7 s (the GPU's check time) 94.0% at 0.4/hr; every 15 s (the CPU's check time, which it falls back to by itself) 92.5% at 0.4/hr. +0.6 checks per camera-hour. CPU backend, scored the same way at its keep-97% cut: one check 89.0% at 0.2/hr; re-check every 15 s (what it actually does, since a check is still pending at 7 s) 91.0% at 0.2/hr (compare_verifiers.py, compare_recheck.txt). Interval set from the backends' check times before the result.
violence._cut_cpu: The cpu backend scores on its own scale (8 images, not a video). Keeps 97% of true alarms, not 98% like the gpu cut: the cpu's camera false alarms cluster at -6.9 to -6.5, right above the 98% cut (-6.78), so that cut is fragile. 97% sits clear of them and costs 1 fight in 200. Chosen after seeing the camera results, so the cross-validated numbers are the honest ones: keep 98% 90.0% at 0.6/hr, keep 97% 89.0% at 0.2/hr.

robbery._enabled: Off since 2026-10-07: robbery_from_fight below caught more robbery (59.4% vs 51.1% of 133 events) with fewer false alarms (0.6 vs 2.0/hr) and far fewer fights mislabelled as robbery (20.5% vs 69%) at about the same number of verifier checks (67 vs 62 per camera-hour incl. fights), so while the verifier runs the robbery model is not run at all; it is the fallback (0.85 x3) whenever the verifier is unavailable. Set true to run both.
robbery._cut_cpu: cpu backend, same rule as the gpu cut (keep 95% of true alarms, fitted on all data; in-sample 50.4% at 0.6/hr). Cross-validated on 133 robbery events + 5 h of held-out cameras: cpu 49.6% at 0.6/hr (AUC 0.986), gpu 51.1% at 2.0/hr (AUC 0.983).

weapon._what: Added 2026-10-14. ARMED THREAT alerts (weapon detector + pose tracking, every one of them) wait for the verifier's weapon question (alarm_verifier.QUESTIONS['weapon']) on a square crop around the person the alert names, cut from full-resolution frames (WEAPON_PAD 0.5, 8 frames over the last 2 s, longest side 448). Passed -> alert with the verdict; rejected -> dropped; check failed or verifier unavailable -> alert exactly as before. No stage-1 setting: the weapon pipeline's own alert rule is the candidate.
weapon._measured: experiments/weapon_alerts (training repo). The app's weapon pipeline replayed on the same 5 h of held-out street cameras as every verifier figure (weapon_alert_eval.py, 12 loop frames/s): 14 ARMED THREAT alerts, 2.8/hr, all 14 looked at and false (phones, bag straps, shirt prints, a belt, market stalls). Cut keeps 98% of real weapons, fitted on the hand-labelled guns and knives of weapons_v2's test set held by a person (1,175, testset_people.py; the same crop as live) -- split in halves, fit on one, scored on the other: 97.9% of weapons kept, 95.2% of small (street-size) guns, 98.9% of knives; held-out camera false alarms 2.8 -> 1.4/hr (only 14 alerts behind that figure); 51% of labelled phones in hand rejected; 5 of 5 clear guns in real robbery CCTV kept. Keep 95% would give 1.0/hr but keep only 86.8% of small guns -- for an armed-threat alarm a missed gun costs more than a false alert. All-data cut here: 7 of the 14 camera alerts left.
weapon._cpu: No cut_cpu yet: on the cpu backend this task cannot run (AlarmVerifier.can_run), so weapon alerts there go out unverified, as before.

robbery_from_fight._what: Added 2026-10-07. No detector of its own: the VIOLENCE ensemble's WHOLE-FRAME score (before person-crop confirmation) at a loose 0.25 x1 gives candidates. A candidate becomes a ROBBERY alert only if BOTH (1) the yes/no robbery question scores >= cut -- it separates crime from calm camera footage (AUC 0.999) but NOT robbery from fight (AUC 0.667; it said yes on 86% of 200 held-out fights) -- AND (2) the multiple-choice question (alarm_verifier.MC_QUESTION: A fight / B robbery / C nothing) gives log P(B) - log P(A) >= mc_cut, the best robbery-vs-fight separator measured (AUC 0.877). (2) is asked only after (1) passed.
robbery_from_fight._measured: experiments/crop_recheck/mc_combined.py, 133 robbery events + 5 h of held-out cameras + 200 held-out fights; both cuts fitted per fold on half the robbery videos only (keep 98% on yes/no, 80% on B-vs-A), never on fights or cameras. Cross-validated: robbery-labelled alerts 59.4% (UCF robbery 62%, shoplifting 78%, street/CamNuvem 28%), robbery false alarms 0.6/hr, fights labelled robbery 20.5%. For comparison: strict robbery model 8.3% / 1.4/hr / 25% of fights; robbery model + yes/no check 51.1% / 2.0/hr / 69%; this path with yes/no only 69.2% / 0.8/hr / 86% (its street 'gain' was the question passing violent clips, not recognising robbery). Keep rates chosen from 8 pairs after seeing results: the highest robbery recall with fights mislabelled no more often than by the old robbery model (25%). All-data cuts here: in-sample 57.1%, 2 camera false alarms in 5 h, 41/200 fights.
robbery_from_fight._cpu: cpu backend (llama.cpp Q4), its own score scale, SAME keep rates as the gpu cuts (98% yes/no, 80% B-vs-A) -- not re-chosen on the cpu results. Cross-validated the same way (mc_combined.py --backend cpu): robbery-labelled alerts 60.9% (UCF robbery 62%, shoplifting 78%, street 36%), robbery false alarms 0.8/hr, fights labelled robbery 22.7% -- vs gpu 59.4% / 0.6/hr / 20.5%. All-data cuts here: in-sample 57.1%, 4 camera false alarms in 5 h, 45/200 fights. The app's cpu backend gives the experiment's scores exactly on both questions (verify_mc_cpu_shipped.py: 10/10 alarms, max difference 0.000) -- only because scored requests are sent with cache_prompt off; with llama-server reusing the yes/no request's cached frames, B-vs-A was off by up to 0.65.

verifier._what: Added 2026-10-07. The fight detector runs at a LOOSER stage-1 setting (tasks.*.stage1_*; robbery candidates come from its whole-frame score, tasks.robbery_from_fight) and every candidate alarm's last 2 s (8 frames, longest side 448) is shown to Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct with a yes/no question; log P(Yes) - log P(No) >= cut lets it through. Passed alerts carry the model's verdict and a one-sentence description (ctx.verifier). maincode/alarm_verifier.py.
verifier._measured: experiments/crop_recheck (training repo): cascade_eval.py + vlm_verify.py, 200 held-out fights / 133 robbery events spliced into street footage + 5 h of held-out street cameras (5 cameras, none ever trained on), cut fitted on half the source videos and scored on the other half. Violence: deployed 0.45 x 2 = 88.0% caught at 1.4 false alarms/hr; 0.25 x 1 + verifier = 90.5% at 0.4/hr. Robbery: deployed 0.85 x 3 = 8.3% at 1.4/hr; robbery model 0.60 x 2 + verifier = 51.1% at 2.0/hr; robbery_from_fight (the fight model's whole-frame candidates, yes/no + robbery-vs-fight questions; what runs now) = 59.4% at 0.6/hr, 20.5% of fights mislabelled robbery. NVIDIA Cosmos-Embed1 (90.0% at 1.6/hr) and Qwen3-VL-4B 4-bit (~32 s per alarm) were measured and not chosen. The cuts here are fitted on ALL the data (98% / 95% of true alarms kept): in-sample 90.5% at 0.6/hr and 50.4% at 1.2/hr.
verifier._cost: Backend gpu: ~4.2 GB VRAM (fp16) on top of the detector stack -- measured together on the GTX 1660 SUPER: peak 5.66 of 6.14 GB with the desktop's own 1.4 GB. ~6.5-7 s per check while the detectors run, so a verified alert arrives ~7 s after the detector fired; its evidence image is the frame from that moment, and the clip's 20 s pre-roll still covers it. Backend cpu: ~2.1 GB RAM, no VRAM, ~15 s per check (see _backend). About 67 checks per camera-hour on street footage (fights 13 + robbery_from_fight 54). Vandalism and weapons are not verified.
verifier._fallback: If the weights are missing, transformers / llama-server is not installed, loading fails, the GPU runs out of memory, a check fails, or more than max_pending candidates are waiting, the affected fight alarms use the detector's ORIGINAL strict setting (violence 0.45 x 2); robbery_from_fight candidates then raise nothing, and while the verifier is down the robbery model runs again at 0.85 x 3 -- the system exactly as measured before this existed. CPU-only machines never load it. Rollback: enabled false.

vandalism_marks._role: Single-frame YOLO detector for graffiti/tags. Feeds static_targets for the vandalism rule and is available as a standalone signal. Listed here so the dev team can see it: it is deployed and live in the pipeline, and a deployed model nobody can see is one nobody checks.
vandalism_marks._edge_band_note: Detections whose centre falls in the top/bottom 12% of frame are dropped. Measured 2026-08-22: 99.5% of this model's 10,710 detections on lyns_restaurant were the burned-in DVR timestamp, while 0.0% of 982 detections across four real graffiti videos fell in those bands. Removes 75.3% of false detections at zero true cost.

camera._index_note: MACHINE-SPECIFIC, do not assume it transfers. On the dev desktop index 5 is the OBS VIRTUAL CAMERA (how test footage is piped in), not a webcam -- index 0 doesn't open there at all. On a laptop or an end-user machine 0 is normally the built-in webcam, which is why 0 is what ships. OBS lands on a different index on every machine, so if you're testing through OBS elsewhere, find its index with the Monitor view's camera picker (POST /set_camera_index) rather than copying 5 across. main.py probes 0-9 when the configured index fails, so a wrong value costs about a second of startup, not a broken camera.
camera._replay_a_file_instead: For repeatable testing, prefer camera.source over an index: any non-numeric value is passed straight to cv2.VideoCapture, so a VIDEO FILE PATH works as a source (e.g. 'D:\\EcoVisionImagesTraining\\ucf_source\\violence\\Assault\\Assault001_x264.mp4'). That removes OBS from the loop entirely, behaves identically on every machine, and replays the exact same footage every run -- which an OBS virtual camera cannot promise. Env override CAMERA_SOURCE does the same without editing this file.
camera._source_by_name: 2026-10-01: a camera can be named instead of numbered. 'OBS Virtual Camera' resolves to whatever index OBS has on THIS machine (5 on the dev desktop, something else elsewhere), via the Windows device list. If no camera by that name exists (a PC without OBS), the core falls back to probing 0-9 and uses the first working camera, so this default is safe to ship. OBS must have Start Virtual Camera pressed or the feed is black. Picking a camera by name in the Monitor view saves it by name here. Set to '' to go back to camera.index.
camera._camera_id_note: 2026-08-19: this physical camera's row id in the `cameras` table (see the Cameras tab / DevTeam console -- 1 is the seeded 'Main Entrance Hub', 2 is 'Sector B Gate'). main.py resolves the REAL, current name for this id via GET /api/camera_name/{id} once at startup, so renaming a camera in the Cameras tab is what actually changes what shows on incidents -- not this file. Set this to whichever registered camera index 5 actually is; if it's neither, register it first.
camera.name: Cogon Core Smartpole Node
camera._name_note: Fallback ONLY, used if camera_id above is unset or doesn't resolve (e.g. backend unreachable at AI-core startup). Not the live source of truth anymore.

esp32._enabled_note: Turned on 2026-08-19 for siren/panic-button hardware testing. Set back to false if running without the pole attached -- with it true, every Confirm/Dismiss click makes a real HTTP call to ip_override below and blocks up to 2s on a connect timeout when nothing answers.
esp32._ip_recovered: 2026-08-19: recovered from git history. This is the ONLY ESP32 address this project has ever used -- unchanged from commit 2bee1ef (2 Jun 2026) onward, first as a hardcoded ESP32_IP, later as this override's fallback. Recorded here so it stops living only in a hardcoded default in backend.py.
esp32._not_actually_static: WARNING: the firmware does NOT set a static IP. hardware/esp32_smartpole_tracker.ino calls WiFi.begin(ssid, password) with no WiFi.config(), i.e. plain DHCP -- so .152 was whatever the router leased, or a DHCP reservation configured on the router itself (outside this repo). If the router was reset or its lease table cleared, this address can change and the siren will silently stop working. See _how_to_make_robust below.
esp32._how_to_make_robust: Three options, worst to best: (1) keep this override and re-check the IP whenever the router changes; (2) add WiFi.config() to the sketch for a real static IP -- must sit OUTSIDE the router's DHCP pool or it will collide; (3) restore auto-discovery, which this project USED to have and lost in a refactor: the old POST /panic did `global ESP32_IP; ESP32_IP = request.client.host`, so the pole taught the backend its own address the first time its panic button was pressed. The current /api/panic_trigger dropped the `request: Request` parameter and no longer does this. Option 3 needs no IP configured anywhere and survives any DHCP change.

networking._fixed_2026-08-19: These were the Docker-compose-only 'backend' hostname, which does not resolve outside a compose network. Docker support (docker-compose.yml, which was the only thing overriding this to a real address for local runs) was removed from this repo -- so this JSON value is now what maincode/main.py actually uses whenever nothing overrides it, and every AI-triggered alert (violence/robbery/vandalism/weapons) was silently failing to reach the backend as a result. electron/main.js still overrides this correctly for the packaged desktop app (via the BACKEND_URL env var, now actually read -- see the matching comment in maincode/main.py), but a plain `python maincode/main.py` / run_dev_system.bat run had nothing to override it, so it needs to be correct here too.
